findings.title: Reject weak Ed25519 public keys before accepting signing configuration
findings.description: TicketVerifier::new checks only AlgorithmFamily::Ed and 32-byte length. It accepts the small-order identity public key (01 followed by 31 zero bytes). The pinned jsonwebtoken RustCrypto backend calls ed25519-dalek VerifyingKey::verify, which accepts the identity-R, zero-S signature for arbitrary messages under that key. Thus a mistakenly configured weak key turns signature verification into unconditional acceptance for otherwise valid scoped claims, including arbitrary subject/session/nonces when a corresponding policy is available. This is conditional on trusted signing configuration containing a weak key; it is not token-controlled key injection.
findings.evidence: A memory-only fixture replaced both configured public keys with the identity point and replaced the signatures with R=identity,S=0, without using any private key. The existing ticket-check binary passed admission, authorized identity/effect, rotation, replay, expiry and revocation stages, then panicked at ticket-check.rs:123 because the fresh unsigned negative unsignedArbitraryNonce was accepted. Probe wrapper exit 0 asserted that precise failure; child exit 101. The generated on-disk public fixture was unchanged by the probe.
findings.requestedChange: Parse every configured public key at construction, reject invalid encodings and weak/small-order points, and use appropriately strict Ed25519 signature validation. Add an unsigned identity-key regression alongside malformed-length configuration tests. Review the exact committed fix independently.

findings.title: Bind VerifiedSession to its admitting TrustDomain and full admitted identity
findings.description: VerifiedSession contains only claims, and with_authorized accepts it from any TrustDomain. The receiving domain checks boot/world/content and only jti->exp membership; it never checks that this exact session/identity was admitted by this domain. Two domains with identical scope but different signing-key trust sets can each admit distinct valid tickets with equal jti/exp. A session from domain A can then authorize in domain B even when B does not trust A's signing key, provided B has a matching current policy for the foreign subject/session/generation. Using the same token in two domains also allows their session handles to be interchanged. A random nonce makes accidental collisions unlikely, but an adversarial or separate trusted issuer can choose that public nonce; nonce equality is not domain provenance.
findings.evidence: Exact-source data flow: VerifiedSession at lines 179-181 has no domain identifier; admit at 257-258 records only nonce/expiry and returns claims; with_authorized at 270-283 checks scope, expiry, nonce/expiry and local policy but never originating domain, admitted subject/session or key trust. Static finding; an attempted standalone executable probe failed to link and is not claimed as dynamic evidence.
findings.requestedChange: Give each TrustDomain an unforgeable instance identity and bind admitted sessions to it, or retain an opaque local admission handle with the complete identity/generation binding. Reject handles from another domain before invoking effects. Test different trusted key sets with equal nonce/expiry and a receiving-domain policy for the foreign identity.

positiveAssessment: Issuer authenticates before connecting, takes the canonical account transaction lock, reauthenticates after waiting, checks account/session consistency, obtains explicit admission using that transaction, signs while locked and returns only after COMMIT. The actual PostgreSQL lock-wait revocation test passed and admission was never invoked for the revoked session.

Issuer rejects non-private/non-Ed25519 keys and invalid kid, copies scope before awaits, uses cryptographic nonces and bounds expiry by session, admission and 30 seconds. Identity comes from the credential owner, not scope input.

Rust restricts EdDSA/type/issuer/audience and configured kid, rejects token key URLs/JWKs/critical extensions, validates scoped claims and canonical generations, rejects rollback clocks, consumes admission nonces and fails closed when policy is missing, expired, denied or on another generation.

Policy snapshots are account/session scoped, limited to a five-second observation interval, monotonic in generation/observation and unable to change allow/deny within one generation. The authorized callback receives the checked claim subject/session rather than caller-selected identity.

CI explicitly runs disposable PostgreSQL issuance before Rust consumption under set -euo pipefail. Ephemeral private keys are not serialized. The runtime remains health-only and does not link vl-security; the issuer has no application route. No live activation was observed.

limitations: This is a partial default-off primitive review, not VL-013 acceptance, deployment approval or evidence that unauthorized game commands cannot persist. Task remains IN_PROGRESS with acceptanceMet false.

A synchronous Rust callback is a caller contract, not a type-enforced effect boundary: generic T can be a Future, and callbacks can copy identity, schedule work or mutate captured unrelated state. The existing docs expressly prohibit async/SQL use. Keep that restriction explicit; require the actual mutation owner to bind target actor and recheck session/policy under its own transaction lock. Do not treat Ok(Future) as authorized completion.

Five-second policy snapshots intentionally permit bounded stale authorization. Session expiry remains capped by ticket expiry; session revocation requires current authenticated policy delivery/generation ownership, which is not implemented. Immediate SQL-bound revocation, persisted receipt/state atomicity and rejection-with-zero-writes remain unproven.

Replay protection is one in-memory owner per boot, not command idempotency, multi-replica fencing or durable replay protection. Boot unpredictability and uniqueness are deployment responsibilities. Policy entries remain capacity bounded without eviction, so a long-lived owner can eventually fail closed at capacity.

No production signing configuration, allocator, authenticated policy transport, Windows/Unity/WSS login or Rust gameplay persistence exists in the reviewed slice. No endpoint or legacy authority cutover is enabled.
